questions.q: In a **bootstrap sample**, rows are drawn **with replacement**. What does that mean in practice?
options: The same row can be picked more than once, and some rows are not picked at all
Each row appears exactly once, just in a shuffled order
Half of the rows are picked, so each model trains on a smaller dataset
Picked rows are replaced with slightly altered synthetic copies
questions.why: After a row is picked it goes back into the pool, so it can be picked again; the sample has the same size n as the original, with some rows doubled and others missing. A mere shuffle would give every model identical data, so averaging would cancel nothing.

questions.q: Which base model is bagging most likely to improve noticeably?
options: A linear regression with a handful of features
A decision stump with a single split
A deep, unpruned decision tree
A model that always predicts the training mean
questions.why: Bagging removes **variance**, and deep unpruned trees are the classic high-variance model: small changes in the data reshape them. Linear regression and stumps are stable (low variance), so their bootstrap copies look alike and averaging them adds computation with little gain.

questions.q: A bag of 100 deep trees scores 86% test accuracy and its **OOB estimate** is 85.5%. What is the most sensible reading?
options: The OOB score is leaking test data, which is why the two numbers agree
The two numbers agree only by chance; OOB scores are not related to test performance
The ensemble is overfitting, because the OOB score is lower than the test score
The OOB estimate is a trustworthy stand-in for unseen-data performance, obtained without a separate validation set
questions.why: Each row's OOB prediction comes only from trees that never saw that row, so the OOB score is an honest estimate of performance on new data; agreeing with the test score is exactly what you hope for. A half-point gap is ordinary noise, not a sign of overfitting.

questions.q: Each tree has prediction variance σ² = 200 and any two trees' errors have correlation ρ = 0.25. Using the bagging variance formula ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ² / B, what is the variance of an average of B = 20 trees?
questions.why: 0.25 × 200 + 0.75 × 200 / 20 = 50 + 7.5 = 57.5. The tempting 10 is σ² / B, which assumes the trees are completely uncorrelated; 50 is only the shared-error floor ρσ² that you would approach with infinitely many trees.

questions.q: A tiny dataset has n = 10 rows. What is the probability that one particular row is **out-of-bag** for a single bootstrap sample?
questions.why: The row must be missed on all 10 draws: (1 − 1/10)¹⁰ = 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.349. The familiar 0.368 is the limit for large n, not the value at n = 10; 0.651 is the chance the row is included at least once.

questions.q: A team grows its bagged ensemble from 200 to 2,000 trees and the validation error barely moves. What is the best explanation?
options: The error has hit the floor set by the correlation between trees (ρσ²), which more trees cannot remove
Too many trees have caused the ensemble to overfit
The bootstrap samples were too small to train useful trees
The trees should have been pruned before averaging
questions.why: Adding trees shrinks only the (1 − ρ)σ² / B term; the shared part ρσ² stays, so returns diminish. The next lever is lowering ρ, which is what random forests do. More trees never cause overfitting in bagging; they only cost time and memory.

questions.q: Interview: "Why does bagging sample n rows with replacement instead of splitting the data into B separate, non-overlapping chunks?" Which answer is best?
options: Sampling with replacement guarantees no row is ever duplicated
Disjoint chunks would make the models more correlated with each other
It keeps each model's training set as large as the original, so each model stays strong while the samples still differ
Sampling with replacement reduces the bias of each individual model
questions.why: Splitting into B chunks would give each model only n / B rows and so much weaker models. The bootstrap keeps every training set at size n yet makes them different, which is what averaging needs. Disjoint chunks would actually make models less alike, not more, and duplication is the point of replacement, not something it avoids.

questions.q: Interview: "You bagged 500 decision stumps and accuracy barely improved on a single stump. Why?" Which answer is best?
options: 500 trees is not enough; bagging stumps needs several thousand
Stumps need feature scaling before they can be bagged
The OOB rows were wasted; you should have used a separate validation set
Stumps are high-bias, low-variance models; bagging removes variance, not bias, so an average of stumps is still too simple
questions.why: Each stump is systematically too simple, and averaging many stable, too-simple models gives a stable, too-simple model. Bagging works best on deep, flexible trees whose errors are large but varied. Adding more stumps cannot fix bias, and trees do not need scaling.
